# db-test-kit-js — complete documentation for language models

Generated from the same Markdown that builds the documentation site. Prefer RECREATE.md when
performing an adoption or update because it is the canonical operational checklist.

# Home

<TransactionSketch />

<div class="home-copy">

<p class="home-kicker">The short version</p>

## Test the application you are actually shipping.

Mock the person who signed in—not the authorization decision. Read shared fixture rows through the
real schema. Create the unusual state with factories. Call the same server function production calls.
Then roll the whole test back.

This is deliberately a reference to copy, not a package to install. Database test infrastructure sits
directly on your application's seams: its connection owner, migrations, schema types, authorization
boundary, and test runner. Those seams should stay visible.

<ol class="home-principles">
  <li><span>01</span><div><strong>A baseline worth knowing</strong><p>A few committed, label-addressed fixtures make the shared world readable without rebuilding it for every test.</p></div></li>
  <li><span>02</span><div><strong>Variation belongs to the test</strong><p>Factories create only what the example changes. Lazy associations keep setup small without making it magical.</p></div></li>
  <li><span>03</span><div><strong>Rollback is the cleanup</strong><p>The test runs inside an interactive transaction. A sentinel throw guarantees that a passing callback never commits.</p></div></li>
</ol>

<div class="home-aside">
  <p class="home-kicker">Honest by construction</p>
  <p><strong>One transaction owns one connection.</strong> That makes isolation cheap. It also means concurrency is fake, database <code>now()</code> is frozen, and an expected SQL error can abort the transaction. The kit pins those facts with tests and gives race-sensitive work an explicit committed-mode exit.</p>
</div>

<p class="home-kicker">Choose your route</p>

## Same design. Two working implementations.

The root project uses **Drizzle + PGlite** for a zero-service first run, then exercises the same suite
against Postgres. The Prisma 7 variant uses real Postgres and carries its own exact toolchain pins,
fixture types, loader, and caveat tests.

  <a href="./guide/prisma"><span>PRISMA 7</span><strong>Start from the tested Postgres variant.</strong><em>Open the Prisma path →</em></a>
</div>

# Quick start

# Quick start

The repository contains two small multi-tenant applications with the same tests. The default project
uses Drizzle and starts with PGlite, so it needs no database service. The Prisma project uses disposable
Postgres.

## Drizzle with zero setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js.git
cd db-test-kit-js
corepack enable
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
```

The suite proves fixture loading, rollback isolation, a tenancy matrix, factories, savepoints,
transaction failure behavior, and the database seam. The concurrency test is skipped because PGlite's
single session cannot demonstrate a real race.

## Drizzle against Postgres

```bash
docker compose up -d
pnpm test:pg
```

This runs the same suite plus `test/tasks.concurrency.test.ts` against a throwaway database.

## Prisma 7 against Postgres

```bash
cd variants/prisma
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
```

The Prisma variant uses its own exact ORM/toolchain pins and lockfile. Its test script generates the
client, deploys migrations, loads the baseline, and runs the suite.

::: warning Use only a disposable test database
Committed-mode tests and fixture bootstrap mutate data outside the per-test rollback transaction.
Never point either project at development, staging, or production. Read [Database safety](/reference/safety)
before adapting the Postgres scripts.
:::

## Next

- [See how the transaction, fixtures, and factories fit together](/guide/how-it-works)
- [Choose an adoption path](/guide/choose-a-path)
- [Give the canonical checklist to an agent](/agents/)

# How it works

# How it works

The kit combines three familiar testing tools and one application seam. None is novel alone; their
composition is the useful part.

For the longer history—including the Rails APIs that directly inspired the fixture model—see
[Design lineage](/reference/lineage/). To begin from working tests instead, browse the
[example walkthroughs](/examples/).

## 1. Rollback isolation

Vitest's `aroundEach` opens an interactive transaction, makes its client current, runs the test, and
throws a private sentinel error. Throwing matters: a transaction callback that returns normally commits.
The outer harness recognizes only its own sentinel and lets every other failure reach Vitest.

Production code continues importing the normal application `db`. In singleton-style applications, the
test setup mocks that one module with a proxy to the current transaction. Access outside a test
transaction throws unless the file explicitly selected committed mode.

## 2. A committed fixture baseline

Fixtures represent the handful of records almost every test can safely read: two tenants, membership
edges, users with different authorization states, and a few domain records. They load once before the
suite, not before each test.

Rows are keyed by labels. IDs are UUIDv5 values derived from the fixture set and label, so relationships
can be declared without querying:

```ts
organizationId: idOf(organizationFixtures, "acme")
```

The label is checked by TypeScript. A misspelling fails typechecking instead of becoming a missing row at
runtime.

## 3. Factories for variation

Factories create state owned by one test. Persistence happens in Fishery's `onCreate`, leaving `build()`
pure. Associations are lazy: a task factory can create its organization and project only when the test
did not provide them.

The rule of thumb is simple:

| Data | Use |
|---|---|
| Read by many tests and rarely changed | Fixture |
| Meaningful only inside one test | Factory |
| A repeated graph or workflow state | Scenario composed from factories |

## 4. A real authorization boundary

The session lookup is fakeable; the tenant or membership check is not. Tests can say `signInAs(user)` and
then call the real server function. The database-backed authorization query, domain query, mutation, and
audit write all happen inside the same rollback transaction.

## 5. An explicit escape hatch

One transaction owns one connection. That is desirable isolation, but it cannot prove behavior that
requires independent transactions. A committed-mode file opts out, creates its own tenant, and runs only
against disposable Postgres. This makes the limitation visible rather than silently weakening a race test.

See [Caveats and escape hatches](/reference/caveats) for the executable boundaries.

---

# Choose an adoption path

# Choose an adoption path

Start with two questions: which ORM owns your transaction client, and how does application code obtain
that client?

| ORM | Application database access | Starting point |
|---|---|---|
| Drizzle | One imported singleton | Root project; mock the seam module |
| Drizzle | Dependency injection | Root project; pass `tx` and skip the module mock |
| Prisma 7 | One imported singleton | `variants/prisma`; mock the seam module |
| Prisma 7 | Dependency injection | `variants/prisma`; pass the interactive client |

## Use the Drizzle path when

- production uses Drizzle with Postgres;
- tests can use `node-postgres`, `postgres-js`, or PGlite for interactive transactions;
- the test process can run the project's migrations.

[Adopt the Drizzle version →](/guide/drizzle)

## Use the Prisma path when

- the project uses Prisma 7 with Postgres;
- a real disposable Postgres database is available;
- the generated client can be produced before tests.

[Adopt the Prisma version →](/guide/prisma)

## Stop before copying when

- the target does not use Postgres;
- database clients are constructed throughout the application instead of behind one seam;
- tests cannot open interactive transactions;
- an existing harness already solves rollback isolation and only fixtures or guard tests are missing.

In the last case, preserve the working harness and add only the missing layers. `RECREATE.md` begins with
this reconnaissance deliberately.

---

# Adopt the Drizzle version

# Adopt the Drizzle version

The root project is the canonical Drizzle implementation. Do not copy its example domain wholesale.
Use the classifications in `RECREATE.md`.

## What normally transfers unchanged

- fixture identity and label helpers;
- fixed fixture clock;
- global setup shape;
- rollback sentinel behavior;
- the test that forbids database access outside a transaction.

## What must match the target

- schema and database module imports;
- migration runner and migrations directory;
- session lookup module;
- seam-guard allow-list;
- fixture rows and dependency order;
- factories and authorization tests;
- test database name, URL, and safety rules.

## Driver boundary

Production may use Neon's HTTP driver while tests use `node-postgres` or PGlite. The requirement is not
that production and tests share a transport; it is that application queries share the same Drizzle schema
and the test driver supports an interactive transaction held open across a test.

## Canonical procedure

Read the complete [`RECREATE.md`](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/RECREATE.md)
before editing a target repository. It includes reconnaissance, the file map, verification failures to
induce deliberately, and pitfalls discovered during cold adoption trials.

---

# Adopt the Prisma version

# Adopt the Prisma version

`variants/prisma/` is a complete Prisma 7 project, not a sketch layered over the Drizzle source. Start
there because the ORM differences affect the harness, fixture types, loader, bootstrap, generated code,
and database requirements.

## Important differences

- Prisma requires real Postgres in this reference; there is no PGlite default.
- The interactive transaction uses explicit `timeout` and `maxWait` values.
- Fixture sets name Prisma delegates and use scalar foreign-key fields.
- Bootstrap runs `prisma generate` and `prisma migrate deploy`.
- Fixture loading uses a plain, unextended client so application extensions cannot reject cleanup.
- Prisma `@default(now())` behavior differs from SQL `DEFAULT now()`; both behaviors are pinned by tests.

## Version policy

The Prisma CLI, client, and adapter are pinned to exactly the same current stable Prisma 7 release. The
variant does not claim Prisma 8 compatibility: that major version changes core APIs and deserves a
separate implementation and test pass, not a widened version range.

## Dependency-injected applications

If application functions already accept a Prisma client, skip `vi.mock`. Pass the current transaction
client to the real functions and keep authorization dependencies real except for the session identity.

Read the [variant README](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/variants/prisma/README.md)
and then follow the Prisma section of `RECREATE.md`.

---

# Update an existing copy

# Update an existing copy

Copied infrastructure needs a visible provenance trail. Every managed COPY or ADAPT file begins with a
header such as:

```ts
// db-test-kit-js v0.2 · ADAPT — copied; adapt only where RECREATE.md says
```

## The update loop

1. Read the copied files' headers. A missing header means the copy predates v0.2.
2. Read every newer entry in `CHANGELOG.md`.
3. Replace changed COPY files from the reference.
4. Apply changed ADAPT files as a three-way comparison, preserving the target's imports and seams.
5. Never overwrite EXAMPLE fixtures, factories, or domain tests.
6. Stamp touched files with the new version. A headerless v0.1→v0.2 update stamps every managed file.
7. Repeat the complete verification checklist, including deliberate failure checks.

The update procedure was tested on a reconstructed v0.1 copy. That trial found the header migration and
typecheck-command ambiguities now documented in the canonical instructions.

For operational details, use [`RECREATE.md`](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/RECREATE.md),
not this overview.

---

# Examples

# Examples

Start with behavior, then follow the code into the repository. Each example shows the smallest useful
excerpt from both implementations when the ORM changes the expression of the pattern.

| Example | What it demonstrates | Start here |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary rollback test | A write is visible now and absent in the next test | [Read the example](/examples/rollback-test) |
| Fixtures + factories | Shared identities plus variation owned by one test | [Read the example](/examples/fixtures-factories) |
| Authorization + tenancy | Fake identity; keep the database authorization decision real | [Read the example](/examples/authorization) |
| Real concurrency | Leave the wrapper transaction when separate connections are the behavior | [Read the example](/examples/concurrency) |

## The recurring shape

```ts
it("exercises the real application", async () => {
  signInAs(fx.users.olivia);                    // replace identity lookup
  const record = await domainFactory.create(); // arrange test-owned variation
  const result = await serverFunction(record); // real auth + real queries
  expect(result).toEqual(expected);             // rollback follows automatically
});
```

There is no cleanup call in an ordinary test. Vitest's `aroundEach` owns the transaction, the application
database import points at that transaction, and the harness forces a rollback after the assertion.

## Browse the complete implementations

- [Drizzle root project](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/tree/main/test)
- [Prisma 7 variant](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/tree/main/variants/prisma/test)
- [Application code under test](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/tree/main/src)

The excerpts explain the design; the repository tests are the executable authority.

---

# Example: a rollback test

# A normal rollback test

The most important example is intentionally uneventful: write through the real application database,
assert the state, and omit cleanup.

```ts{2-3}
it("a test's writes are visible to it...", async () => {
  await db.update(users).set({ name: "Changed" }).where(eq(users.id, fx.users.olivia.id));
  await userFactory.create({ name: "RolledBack" });

  const [olivia] = await db.select().from(users).where(eq(users.id, fx.users.olivia.id));
  expect(olivia.name).toBe("Changed");
});
```

The next test sees the committed baseline again:

```ts{2,4}
it("...and gone in the next test", async () => {
  const [olivia] = await db.select().from(users).where(eq(users.id, fx.users.olivia.id));
  expect(olivia.name).toBe("Olivia Owner");
  expect(await db.select().from(users).where(eq(users.name, "RolledBack"))).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

The test did not reset the user or delete the factory record. The surrounding transaction was discarded.

## What wraps the test

```ts{1,3}
aroundEach(async (runTest) => {
  try {
    await inRolledBackTransaction(runTest);
  } finally {
    signOut();
  }
});
```

Inside the harness, a private error forces rollback because an interactive transaction callback that
returns normally would commit:

```ts{7}
await committedDb().transaction(async (tx) => {
  current = tx as unknown as TestDatabase;
  try {
    await runTest();
  } finally {
    current = undefined;
  }
  throw new Rollback();
});
```

## Full source

- [Drizzle fixture and rollback tests](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/test/fixtures.test.ts)
- [Drizzle transaction setup](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/test/db/setup.ts)
- [Drizzle harness](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/test/db/harness.ts)
- [Prisma fixture and rollback tests](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/variants/prisma/test/fixtures.test.ts)
- [Prisma harness](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/variants/prisma/test/db/harness.ts)

# Example: fixtures and factories

# Fixtures and factories together

Fixtures answer “which known actor or tenant?” Factories answer “what unusual state does this test own?” A
test can use both without rebuilding the shared world.

```ts{3,6}
it("creates a project for a member created by a factory", async () => {
  // A new tenant and user belong only to this test.
  const membership = await memberFactory.owner().create();

  signInAs(membership.user);
  const id = await createProject(membership.organizationId, "Fresh");

  expect((await listProjects(membership.organizationId)).map((p) => p.id)).toEqual([id]);
});
```

For a shared relationship, pass a fixture ID into the factory instead of creating another tenant:

```ts{2}
const task = await taskFactory.create({
  organizationId: fx.organizations.acme.id,
  title: "Review the release",
});
```

The label `acme` carries meaning across tests. The task does not; it rolls back with this test.

## A readable fixture relationship

```ts{3}
export const projectFixtures = fixtures(projects, "projects", {
  website: {
    organizationId: idOf(organizationFixtures, "acme"),
    name: "Website",
    createdAt: FIXTURE_EPOCH,
  },
});
```

`idOf()` checks the label at compile time and computes the ID without first querying the database.

## Full source

- [Drizzle project tests](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/test/projects.test.ts)
- [Drizzle fixtures](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/tree/main/test/fixtures)
- [Drizzle factories](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/tree/main/test/factories)
- [Prisma project tests](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/variants/prisma/test/projects.test.ts)
- [Prisma fixtures](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/tree/main/variants/prisma/test/fixtures)
- [Prisma factories](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/tree/main/variants/prisma/test/factories)

For the design rules behind these choices, see [Fixtures](/reference/fixtures) and
[Factories](/reference/factories).

# Example: authorization and tenancy

# Authorization and tenancy

The session lookup is a controlled test seam. The membership query, tenant filter, domain query, and audit
write remain real.

## One matrix, several boundaries

```ts
it("rejects a signed-out caller", async () => {
  await expect(listProjects(fx.organizations.acme.id)).rejects.toThrow("Not authenticated");
});

it("rejects a signed-in user who isn't a member", async () => {
  signInAs(fx.users.ned);
  await expect(listProjects(fx.organizations.acme.id)).rejects.toThrow("Not a member");
});

it("doesn't leak another org's project", async () => {
  signInAs(fx.users.olivia);
  expect(await getProject(fx.organizations.acme.id, fx.projects.secret.id)).toBeNull();
  await expect(listProjects(fx.organizations.other.id)).rejects.toThrow("Not a member");
});
```

These are application tests, not controller mocks. They call the same functions production calls against
the real schema.

## ORM-specific assertion, same behavior

::: code-group

```ts [Drizzle]
const logs = await db
  .select()
  .from(auditLogs)
  .where(eq(auditLogs.resourceId, fx.projects.website.id));
expect(logs[0]).toMatchObject({ actorUserId: fx.users.olivia.id, action: "view" });
```

```ts [Prisma]
const logs = await prisma.auditLog.findMany({
  where: { resourceId: fx.projects.website.id },
});
expect(logs[0]).toMatchObject({ actorUserId: fx.users.olivia.id, action: "view" });
```

:::

The assertion changes with the client API. The authorization boundary does not.

## Full source

- [Drizzle tenancy suite](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/test/projects.test.ts)
- [Prisma tenancy suite](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/variants/prisma/test/projects.test.ts)
- [Application membership boundary](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/src/membership.ts)
- [Test session seam](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/test/auth/session.ts)

# Example: real concurrency

# Real concurrency

One rollback transaction owns one connection. That is excellent isolation, but simultaneous promises on
that client do not demonstrate independent transactions racing. A concurrency test opts out explicitly.

```ts{1,7-12}
useCommittedDb();

it("exactly one of several simultaneous claims wins", async () => {
  const task = await taskFactory.create();
  const members = await Promise.all(
    [1, 2, 3, 4].map(() => memberFactory.create({ organizationId: task.organizationId })),
  );

  const results = await Promise.all(
    members.map(async (membership) => {
      signInAs(membership.user);
      return claimTask(task.organizationId, task.id);
    }),
  );

  expect(results.filter(Boolean)).toHaveLength(1);
});
```

`useCommittedDb()` is file-scoped. Factories now commit, so this suite creates an isolated tenant rather
than changing shared fixture rows. The Drizzle root skips the test unless it is running against real
Postgres; the in-process PGlite path has only one session.

## Why this is separate

```ts
describe.skipIf(!usingRealPostgres)("claimTask (concurrent)", () => {
  // independent application calls can now use independent pool connections
});
```

This is not a slower version of every test. It is a targeted escape hatch for behavior whose subject is
commit visibility, locks, or races.

## Full source

- [Drizzle concurrency test](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/test/tasks.concurrency.test.ts)
- [Prisma concurrency test](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/variants/prisma/test/tasks.concurrency.test.ts)
- [Drizzle claim implementation](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/src/tasks.ts)
- [Prisma claim implementation](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/variants/prisma/src/tasks.ts)

See [Caveats and escape hatches](/reference/caveats) for the other boundaries pinned by tests.

---

# Fixtures

# Fixtures

Fixtures are the small, committed world that many tests are allowed to read. They load once before the
suite and survive each test's rollback. Use them for stable identities and relationships that make tests
easier to understand: two tenants, users with distinct roles, membership edges, and a representative
domain record or two.

Use a [factory](/reference/factories) when a record exists only to arrange one test.

## The decision rule

| Put it in a fixture when… | Build it with a factory when… |
|---|---|
| Many tests need the same identity | One test owns the record |
| Its label carries domain meaning | Its exact values are the variation under test |
| It should be present before the test starts | The test should create or mutate it |
| Relationships are shared reference context | The graph is specific to one scenario |

Keep the baseline deliberately boring. A large fixture universe creates invisible coupling: changing one
row can affect unrelated tests, and tests stop explaining the state they actually need.

## Declare a fixture set

Each table gets one file. `fixtures()` checks every row against the table's insert type and adds a stable
ID derived from the fixture-set name and label.

```ts
import { organizations } from "@/schema";
import { FIXTURE_EPOCH } from "./clock";
import { fixtures } from "./runtime";

export const organizationFixtures = fixtures(organizations, "organizations", {
  acme: { name: "Acme", slug: "fx-acme", createdAt: FIXTURE_EPOCH },
  other: { name: "Other Co", slug: "fx-other", createdAt: FIXTURE_EPOCH },
});
```

Prefer a fixed fixture clock over `new Date()`. Stable data makes snapshots, ordering, and failure output
repeatable.

## Refer to relationships by label

Use `idOf()` for foreign keys. The fixture-set argument scopes identity, and TypeScript verifies the label.

```ts
import { projects } from "@/schema";
import { organizationFixtures } from "./organizations";
import { fixtures, idOf } from "./runtime";

export const projectFixtures = fixtures(projects, "projects", {
  website: {
    organizationId: idOf(organizationFixtures, "acme"),
    name: "Website",
  },
});
```

`idOf(organizationFixtures, "acmee")` fails typechecking. The loader also rejects a reference whose row is
not included in the loaded fixture sets.

## Export a readable test API

`test/fixtures/index.ts` exposes rows through `fx` and lists fixture sets in foreign-key order:

```ts
export const fx = {
  organizations: organizationFixtures.rows,
  users: userFixtures.rows,
  projects: projectFixtures.rows,
};

export const allFixtureSets = [
  organizationFixtures,
  userFixtures,
  projectFixtures,
];
```

Tests can then say `fx.users.olivia.id` or `fx.organizations.acme.id`. Parents must precede children in
`allFixtureSets`; the loader deletes in reverse order and inserts forward.

## Loading and mutation

The suite-level setup loads fixtures into committed state. Ordinary tests may read them and can even update
or delete them inside the test transaction—the rollback restores the committed row afterward. Do not
mutate fixture objects in JavaScript, and do not let a committed-mode test alter baseline rows.

The loader is idempotent for its own deterministic IDs: it removes those rows, then inserts the declared
sets. It is not a general database reset. The database safety checks still apply.

## Rails lineage

The model comes directly from Rails fixtures: named shared records, label-based relationships, stable IDs,
and transactional tests that return to the committed baseline. This implementation uses typed TypeScript
modules and UUIDv5 instead of YAML/ERB and Active Record accessors. See
[Rails testing ecosystem](/reference/lineage/rails) for the detailed comparison.

## Copy-ready review prompt

```text
Review this repository's database-test fixtures using
https://danielrose7.github.io/db-test-kit-js/reference/fixtures and
https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/RECREATE.md as the standard. Identify fixture rows
that are test-specific and should become factories, unstable timestamps or generated values, raw
foreign-key IDs that should use typed label references, incorrect parent-before-child load order, mutation
of fixture objects, and committed-mode tests that can modify the shared baseline. Report findings with
file paths and line numbers. Do not edit files, run destructive database commands, or assume that
production and test databases are interchangeable.
```

---

# Factories

# Factories

Factories create variation owned by one test. They provide useful defaults while keeping the test free to
override the values that matter. In this kit, Fishery supplies the factory API and the application's real
ORM writes the record inside the current rollback transaction.

Use a [fixture](/reference/fixtures) for a stable record that many tests share.

## Build and create mean different things

`build()` returns a plain object and must not touch the database. `create()` runs the `onCreate` callback,
persists through the application database seam, and returns the created record.

```ts
import { Factory } from "fishery";
import { db } from "@/db";
import { newId } from "@/id";
import { organizations } from "@/schema";

interface OrganizationBuild {
  name: string;
  slug: string;
}

interface OrganizationRecord extends OrganizationBuild {
  id: string;
}

export const organizationFactory = Factory.define<
  OrganizationBuild,
  unknown,
  OrganizationRecord
>(({ sequence, onCreate }) => {
  onCreate(async (build) => {
    const id = newId();
    await db.insert(organizations).values({ id, ...build });
    return { ...build, id };
  });

  return {
    name: `Org ${sequence}`,
    slug: `org-${sequence}-${newId().slice(-6)}`,
  };
});
```

```ts
const draft = organizationFactory.build({ name: "Not persisted" });
const saved = await organizationFactory.create({ name: "Persisted in this test" });
```

Keeping `build()` pure makes it safe for unit tests, request payloads, and expected values. It also makes a
database write visible at the call site through `await ...create()`.

## Lazy associations

A factory may create required related records, but only when the caller did not supply them. This keeps the
convenient path short without forcing every test into a wasteful or irrelevant object graph.

```ts
onCreate(async (build) => {
  const organizationId =
    build.organizationId ?? (await organizationFactory.create()).id;

  const projectId = newId();
  await db.insert(projects).values({
    id: projectId,
    organizationId,
    name: "Factory project",
  });

  const id = newId();
  await db.insert(tasks).values({ id, projectId, organizationId, title: build.title });
  return { ...build, id, projectId, organizationId };
});
```

When a shared fixture is the right parent, pass it explicitly:

```ts
const task = await taskFactory.create({
  organizationId: fx.organizations.acme.id,
  title: "Review the release",
});
```

The created task and any lazily created associations roll back together after the test.

## Defaults, sequences, and traits

- Give every required field a valid default so the shortest factory call creates a valid record.
- Use `sequence` or project ID helpers for uniqueness; do not rely on wall-clock time.
- Use traits for a small number of meaningful, reusable states—not as a second domain model.
- Accept explicit association IDs so callers can prevent implicit record creation.
- Return the values actually persisted, including generated IDs and resolved associations.

## Failure modes

Watch for factories that import an unmocked database client, write during `build()`, eagerly create an
entire graph, hide authorization setup, or return a shape different from the stored row. The harness's seam
guard should make the first mistake fail loudly outside a current transaction.

Factory defaults should not become an unofficial fixture baseline. If many tests repeatedly create the
same meaningful identity, promote only that stable context to a fixture and keep the variable records local.

## factory_bot lineage

Fishery is explicitly inspired by factory_bot. This kit adopts factories, overrides, sequences, traits,
and associations while adding an application-specific persistence boundary in `onCreate`. See
[Rails testing ecosystem](/reference/lineage/rails) and [TypeScript prior art](/reference/lineage/typescript).

## Copy-ready review prompt

```text
Review this repository's database-test factories using
https://danielrose7.github.io/db-test-kit-js/reference/factories and
https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/RECREATE.md as the standard. Verify that build
operations are pure, persistence occurs only in create hooks, database writes use the transaction-aware
application seam, required associations are created lazily and can be supplied explicitly, defaults
produce valid records, returned values match persisted values, and repeated shared identities belong in
fixtures instead. Report findings with file paths and line numbers. Do not edit files or run destructive
database commands.
```

---

# Caveats and escape hatches

# Caveats and escape hatches

The harness makes transaction behavior fast and convenient; it does not repeal transaction semantics.
Each boundary below is pinned by a test in both variants where applicable.

## Expected failures abort transactions

Postgres marks a transaction aborted after a failed statement. Wrap an error you intend to catch in an
application-level nested transaction/savepoint. Be especially careful when application code catches its
own insert error and then tries another query.

## One connection is not concurrency

Queries issued through the wrapping transaction share one connection. A `Promise.all` can appear to pass
while operations actually serialize. Move race-sensitive assertions into a committed-mode file and run
them against real Postgres with data scoped to a tenant created by that test.

## Database time belongs to the transaction

Postgres `now()` is the transaction start time. Rows inserted later in the same test may receive identical
timestamps. Set explicit timestamps when order matters. Prisma's client-side `@default(now())` behaves
differently; raw SQL time still follows Postgres.

## Baselines are visible globally

Cross-tenant jobs and sweep queries see committed fixtures. Keep fixture dates in the past and workflow
states terminal. Scope assertions to the test tenant instead of assuming the whole database is empty.

## Committed mode leaves data behind

The real-Postgres database is disposable per run. A committed-mode test must create a unique tenant and
must never depend on another committed test's cleanup.

---

# Database safety

# Database safety

The default PGlite suite stores its database in the test process. The Postgres and Prisma paths can run
migrations, delete fixture tables, and commit data. Treat their connection strings as destructive input.

## Required posture

- Use a dedicated disposable database created for the test run.
- Give its role access only to that database.
- Name the database unmistakably as a test database.
- Keep production and staging secrets unavailable to test jobs.
- Print the selected host and database before destructive setup.
- Fail closed when the environment does not explicitly identify itself as testing.
- Never “make the tests pass” by weakening a connection-string guard.

## CI isolation

The included workflow creates a Postgres service container visible only to the job. That is the preferred
shape: migrations and committed-mode tests cannot reach application data because no application database
credential exists in the job.

## Target-repository checklist

Before loading fixtures, confirm all of these:

- `NODE_ENV` is `test`;
- the URL is not a production, preview, staging, or development URL;
- the database is disposable;
- migrations point at the same URL the tests use;
- cleanup and committed-mode tests cannot run against a shared database;
- the fixture role cannot connect to production.

The reference is adding executable URL guards before its first public release. Until those land, the
organizational isolation above is mandatory rather than optional.

---

# Compatibility

# Compatibility

This project follows current stable releases rather than maximizing backward compatibility. “Tested”
means exercised by the reference projects, not merely allowed by a version range.

| Component | Tested reference | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| Node.js | 24 | Current stable/LTS line used by CI |
| pnpm | 11.25.0 | Exact package-manager declaration |
| TypeScript | 7.0.2 | Current stable used by both variants |
| Vitest | 5.0.4 | Current stable; `aroundEach` requires at least 4.1 |
| Drizzle ORM | 0.45.4 | Current stable at the last verification |
| PGlite | 0.5.10 | Zero-setup Drizzle backend |
| Prisma | 7.10.0 | Exact CLI/client/adapter pins in the variant |
| Postgres | 16 | Local scripts and CI service image |

Run `pnpm outdated` before a release. ORM, test-runner, and database upgrades require the full caveat
suite and deliberate-failure checks; they should not be treated as lockfile-only maintenance.

## Explicit non-goals

- MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB, and non-Postgres Drizzle dialects;
- Prisma 8 until a dedicated variant is implemented and verified;
- transparent support for arbitrary database client construction;
- preserving support for old runners at the expense of the primary implementation.

Older Vitest and Jest projects can use the hook-pair pattern in `RECREATE.md`, but the reference itself
tracks the current stable Vitest design.

---

# Sources and prior art

# Sources and prior art

Last reviewed: **October 15, 2026**. Version-sensitive behavior is also pinned by executable tests;
documentation links provide context but do not replace those tests.

This page is the compact source index. [Design lineage](/reference/lineage/) explains what the kit takes
from each ecosystem, what it changes, and what it deliberately leaves behind.

## Primary documentation

- [Vitest Test API](https://vitest.dev/api/test) — `aroundEach`, scoped fixtures, concurrency and
  runner behavior.
- [VitePress deployment guide](https://vitepress.dev/guide/deploy) — static GitHub Pages build and
  repository base paths.
- [Drizzle with PGlite](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/connect-pglite) — the zero-service database
  used by the default reference suite.
- [Drizzle Seed](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/seed-overview) — deterministic generated data. It is a
  neighboring tool, not the same thing as a small label-addressed committed fixture baseline.
- [Prisma 7 integration testing](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/prisma-client/testing/integration-testing)
  — official real-database setup and suite-level seed/cleanup approach.
- [Prisma 7 transactions](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/prisma-client/queries/transactions) —
  interactive transaction limits and options.
- [PostgreSQL transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) —
  database semantics beneath both ORM implementations.

## Framework precedents

- [Rails `ActiveRecord::FixtureSet`](https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/FixtureSet.html)
  — label-based fixtures, stable IDs, associations, shared defaults and transactional tests.
- [Django transactions in tests](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/testing/tools/#django.test.TestCase)
  — isolation through transactions and rollback.
- [Laravel database testing](https://laravel.com/docs/database-testing) — factories, seeders and
  database refresh patterns.
- [Fishery](https://github.com/thoughtbot/fishery) — factory_bot-inspired TypeScript factories.

## Closest JavaScript prior art

- [`jest-prisma`](https://github.com/Quramy/jest-prisma) — transaction-per-test and Prisma client seam.
- [`vitest-environment-prisma-postgres`](https://github.com/codepunkt/vitest-environment-prisma-postgres)
  — maintained work extending the same family of Prisma/Vitest transaction patterns.

## Evidence boundary

The project is a TypeScript port and composition of established testing practices, not a claim to have
invented transactional tests, fixtures, or factories. Its original contribution is the worked combination:
two current ORM examples, typed label references, a deliberate application database seam, real tenancy
checks, executable caveat tests, committed-mode concurrency, and agent-readable adoption/update guidance.

Performance claims should be framed qualitatively unless accompanied by a reproducible project-specific
measurement. Transaction rollback avoids schema-wide cleanup work, so the advantage generally becomes more
meaningful as a schema and suite grow; exact ratios depend on the database, schema, hardware and workload.

---

# Design lineage

# Design lineage

db-test-kit-js is a TypeScript composition of mature database-testing practices. Its strongest lineage is
Rails: a small committed fixture baseline, human-readable labels, deterministic identifiers, factories for
variation, and a transaction rolled back after each test. Django and Laravel provide independent evidence
that transaction-backed isolation is a durable framework pattern rather than a Rails peculiarity.

The labels below keep the attribution precise:

- **Direct lineage** means an API or design in this kit was consciously adapted from that source.
- **Parallel precedent** means another ecosystem arrived at a similar practice independently.
- **Kit-specific adaptation** means integration work needed to make the practice explicit and safe in a
  Vitest, TypeScript, ORM, and application-module environment.

## Idea map

| Idea in this kit | Lineage | Where it appears here | Material difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| One rollback transaction per test | Rails direct lineage; Django and Laravel parallel precedent | `test/db/harness.ts`, `test/db/setup.ts` | A private thrown sentinel guarantees the ORM callback rolls back instead of committing |
| A small committed baseline | Rails fixtures direct lineage | `test/fixtures/`, global setup | Fixtures are typed TypeScript rows rather than YAML interpreted by the ORM |
| Stable IDs derived from labels | Rails `FixtureSet.identify` direct lineage | `test/fixtures/identify.ts` | UUIDv5 incorporates fixture-set identity as well as the label |
| Relationships written as label references | Rails fixture labels direct lineage | `idOf(fixtureSet, "label")` | TypeScript checks that the label belongs to that fixture set |
| Factories, traits, and lazy associations | factory_bot direct lineage, via Fishery | `test/factories/` | Persistence is isolated in `onCreate`; `build()` remains pure |
| Explicit non-transactional tests | Rails opt-out direct lineage | `useCommittedDb()` and committed-mode suites | The escape hatch is restricted to disposable Postgres and owns cleanup |
| Database reset alternatives | Django and Laravel parallel precedent | Caveat guidance and committed-mode cleanup | The kit does not hide truncation or migration behind its default path |
| Current-transaction application seam | Kit-specific adaptation | mocked application `db` module and transaction context | Production imports keep working while tests fail closed outside a transaction |
| Real authorization queries in tests | Kit-specific composition | session helper plus real membership query | Only identity lookup is replaceable; database authorization remains real |
| Executable caveats and update headers | Kit-specific maintenance design | caveat tests, managed headers, `RECREATE.md` | The copied implementation carries its own boundaries and provenance |

## Why Rails is the primary reference

Rails joins the relevant ideas into one established workflow. Transactional tests preserve a known
database state; fixture labels describe shared records; `identify` turns a label into a stable ID; and the
factory_bot ecosystem covers data that should vary per test. That combination is closer to this kit than
any single JavaScript package.

This is a port of the *testing model*, not of Rails syntax or global conventions. The kit keeps the useful
division of responsibilities while exposing the database seam, transaction lifetime, opt-out path, and
copy/update boundary as ordinary project code.

Continue with [Rails testing ecosystem](/reference/lineage/rails), then compare
[Django and Laravel](/reference/lineage/frameworks) and the available
[TypeScript prior art](/reference/lineage/typescript).

## Copy-ready research prompt

```text
Read the Design lineage section of the db-test-kit-js documentation, beginning at
https://danielrose7.github.io/db-test-kit-js/reference/lineage/. Follow only its primary-source links.
Produce a table with one row per db-test-kit-js feature and columns for classification (direct lineage,
parallel precedent, or kit-specific adaptation), upstream source, local implementation file, and important
semantic difference. Treat the repository's executable tests as the authority for current implementation
behavior. Do not claim that db-test-kit-js invented transactional tests, fixtures, deterministic fixture
IDs, or factories. Do not make numerical performance claims unless you also provide a reproducible
benchmark and environment details.
```

# Rails testing ecosystem

# Rails testing ecosystem

Last reviewed against Rails **8.1.2** on October 15, 2026.

Rails is the principal inspiration for this kit. The correspondence is not “Rails has tests too”; it is a
specific data model for tests: committed shared fixtures, stable label-addressed identity, per-test
transactions, and factories for local variation.

## Transactional tests

Rails runs tests in database transactions by default and rolls those transactions back after the test.
That restores the committed starting state without deleting every inserted row or rebuilding the schema.
Rails also supports opting out when the behavior under test cannot live inside the wrapper transaction.

db-test-kit-js adapts that lifecycle to Vitest's `aroundEach` and ORM callback APIs. The harness deliberately
throws a private sentinel after the test body because a normally returned interactive-transaction callback
commits. Only that exact sentinel is swallowed; application and assertion errors still fail the test.

Primary source: [Testing Rails Applications — Transactions](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/testing.html#transactions).

## Fixtures as the common case

Rails fixtures are predefined records loaded into the test database. Rails guidance positions them as
shared default data, not as a way to spell every object a test might need. That boundary is retained here:
fixtures cover the small, stable world many tests read; factories create records owned by one test.

The kit does not copy Rails' YAML and ERB format. Fixture modules are TypeScript values checked against the
application schema, and loader order is explicit.

Primary source: [Testing Rails Applications — Fixtures](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/testing.html#the-low-down-on-fixtures).

## Labels and deterministic identity

`ActiveRecord::FixtureSet.identify(label)` gives a fixture label a stable identifier. Rails also lets one
fixture refer to another by label, so relationships remain readable rather than embedding opaque IDs.

The kit ports both ideas. `identify(fixtureSet, label)` derives a UUIDv5 from the fixture-set name and label;
`idOf(fixtureSet, label)` preserves that readability while making an invalid label a TypeScript error. The
fixture-set component prevents identical labels in different tables from sharing an ID.

Primary source: [ActiveRecord::FixtureSet](https://api.rubyonrails.org/v8.1.2/classes/ActiveRecord/FixtureSet.html).

## Factories as the complement

factory_bot is not Rails core, but it is the most direct ancestor of the factory half of the design. Its
factories provide defaults, traits describe reusable variations, and associations build related records.
Fishery brings that vocabulary to TypeScript.

db-test-kit-js adds one firm boundary: `build()` is pure and persistence happens in `onCreate`. Lazy
associations avoid creating a related graph when a test supplies an existing record.

Primary sources: [factory_bot factory reference](https://thoughtbot.github.io/factory_bot/ref/factory.html),
[traits with associations](https://thoughtbot.github.io/factory_bot/traits/with-associations.html), and
[association reference](https://thoughtbot.github.io/factory_bot/ref/association.html).

## What this kit deliberately does not port

- YAML/ERB fixture evaluation and model-shaped global fixture accessors.
- Implicit application database replacement that can silently miss a second connection.
- A claim that one wrapper transaction can test behavior requiring independent transactions.
- Framework-owned magic that an application cannot inspect, copy, or adapt.

The result should feel familiar to a Rails tester while remaining ordinary, explicit TypeScript.

---

# Django and Laravel precedents

# Django and Laravel precedents

Django and Laravel are **parallel precedents**, not the direct source of the kit's API. Both reinforce the
same architectural lesson: database isolation is a first-class test-runner concern, while fixtures,
seeders, and factories serve different data-shaping jobs.

## Django

Django's `TestCase` provides transaction-backed isolation and restores a known starting state. Its
`fixtures` class attribute loads named data files for a test class. `TransactionTestCase` exists for tests
that must observe transaction behavior directly, accepting the cost of resetting the database differently.

The parallel with db-test-kit-js is the distinction between a fast default isolation path and an explicit
path for transaction-sensitive behavior. The kit's `useCommittedDb()` is not a port of Django's class API,
but it serves the same honesty: a wrapper transaction must not be used to “prove” cross-transaction behavior.

Primary source: [Django 6.1 testing tools](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/testing/tools/).

## Laravel

Laravel's `RefreshDatabase` uses a transaction when the schema is current. Its documentation contrasts
that with full migration or truncation approaches, which perform more reset work. Laravel also separates
model factories from seeders: factories make test-specific records, while seeders populate broader known
data.

That resembles this kit's fixture/factory division, although the APIs and loading lifecycle differ. The
kit loads a compact committed baseline once, then rolls back factory-created variation after each test.

Primary source: [Laravel 13 database testing](https://laravel.com/framework/docs/13.x/database-testing).

## What the comparison supports

Across Rails, Django, and Laravel, the recurring design is more important than any exact method name:

1. Establish a known database state.
2. Isolate ordinary tests with transactions when the database and test shape allow it.
3. Use a separate, explicit strategy for tests that must commit or coordinate connections.
4. Keep reusable baseline data distinct from per-test variation.

db-test-kit-js packages those decisions as copyable project code because the TypeScript ecosystem does not
provide one framework-owned lifecycle shared by Vitest, every ORM, and every application database seam.

---

# TypeScript prior art

# TypeScript prior art

The TypeScript ecosystem contains strong pieces of this design, but they live at different layers. This kit
combines them into a worked application pattern and keeps the seams visible.

## Runner and factory building blocks

- [Vitest's Test API](https://vitest.dev/api/test) supplies `aroundEach`, scoped hooks, and the concurrency
  model used by the harness.
- [Fishery](https://github.com/thoughtbot/fishery) supplies factory_bot-inspired factories for TypeScript.
- [Drizzle Seed](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/seed-overview) supplies deterministic generated data. It is
  useful neighboring work, but it is not the same abstraction as a small, committed, label-addressed
  fixture baseline.

## Transaction-focused packages

- [`jest-prisma`](https://github.com/Quramy/jest-prisma) demonstrates transaction-per-test isolation and a
  Prisma client seam in Jest.
- [`vitest-environment-prisma-postgres`](https://github.com/codepunkt/vitest-environment-prisma-postgres)
  continues that family of ideas for Prisma, Postgres, and Vitest.
- [Prisma's integration-testing guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/prisma-client/testing/integration-testing)
  documents real-database setup with suite-level seed and cleanup.

These projects should be preferred when their abstraction matches the application. db-test-kit-js is most
useful as a reference when the team wants the whole pattern in its own repository: baseline fixtures,
factories, a current-transaction seam, real authorization coverage, committed-mode escape hatches, and
executable caveat tests.

## The kit-specific integration work

The novel value claimed here is deliberately narrow. It is not transactions, fixtures, or factories. It is
the documented combination and the safety boundary around a copy-owned implementation:

- ORM-specific harnesses that fail closed when code uses the database outside the active test transaction.
- Typed fixture labels and deterministic IDs that work across Drizzle and Prisma examples.
- An authorization test seam that replaces identity lookup without replacing the database decision.
- Tests that demonstrate nested transaction, connection, timer, and concurrency limitations.
- Version headers and an update procedure that distinguish managed reference code from local adaptations.

See [Sources and prior art](/reference/sources) for the compact link index and
[Compatibility](/reference/compatibility) for versions pinned by the executable examples.

---

# Agent guide

# Agent guide

The repository is designed to be legible to coding agents without requiring the rendered site.

## Copy-ready prompts

Every prompt on this site is intended to work as a single copy-and-paste block. Paths and commands are
included in the prompt itself; surrounding prose is context, not a hidden instruction.

### Adopt the pattern

Give an agent this prompt:

```text
Read https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/RECREATE.md completely. Recreate the
applicable database-testing pattern in this repository. First report the existing database seam,
migration path, ORM, transaction support, authorization boundary, test runner, and any existing
harness/factories. Preserve working pieces and add only what is missing. Run every applicable Step 5
check, including the deliberate failing-test and seam-guard failure checks, and report exactly what ran.
```

### Update a copied implementation

```text
Read the "Updating an existing copy" section at
https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/RECREATE.md#updating-an-existing-copy and every
newer entry in https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md than the version
headers in this repository. Preserve all target-specific ADAPT changes and every EXAMPLE file. Apply only
the reference delta, update the managed headers, and run the complete verification checklist. Before
editing, summarize the files you expect to change. After editing, list every changed file, every check you
ran, and any check you could not run. Do not publish a package or change production data.
```

### Ask an agent to explain the lineage

```text
Read https://danielrose7.github.io/db-test-kit-js/reference/lineage/ and its Rails ecosystem, Django and
Laravel, and TypeScript prior art child pages.
Explain which parts of the kit are direct adaptations of established framework practices, which are
parallel precedents, and which are kit-specific TypeScript integration work. Cite the primary source links
from those files. Do not describe db-test-kit-js as the inventor of transactional tests, fixtures, or
factories, and do not make numerical performance claims without a reproducible benchmark.
```

## Machine-readable entry points

- [`llms.txt`](https://danielrose7.github.io/db-test-kit-js/llms.txt) is the short index.
- [`llms-full.txt`](https://danielrose7.github.io/db-test-kit-js/llms-full.txt) concatenates the documentation into one text resource.
- [`RECREATE.md`](https://github.com/danielrose7/db-test-kit-js/blob/main/RECREATE.md) is canonical for actions.
- `skill/db-test-kit/SKILL.md` mirrors `RECREATE.md` for Agent Skills-compatible tools.

## Rules agents should not infer away

- Do not publish or install the kit as a package.
- Do not mock the authorization decision.
- Do not access the application singleton outside the current transaction.
- Do not run destructive setup against a non-disposable database.
- Do not use a rollback test to claim concurrent behavior was tested.
- Do not overwrite domain-specific fixtures and factories during an update.
